problemText: In 1949 the United States and its Western European partners formed NATO, a military alliance for their common defense. In 1955 the Soviet Union and its Eastern European allies answered with a military alliance of their own. What was it called?
choices: The Marshall Plan
The Non-Aligned Movement
The Warsaw Pact
The European Coal and Steel Community
hints: The name comes from the capital city of Poland, where the treaty was signed.

problemText: The Truman Doctrine of 1947 promised American support to peoples resisting armed takeover, and the Marshall Plan from 1948 sent roughly 13 billion dollars to rebuild Western European economies. Both are described as instruments of containment. What did containment mean?
choices: Withdrawing American forces from Europe so that no confrontation could occur
Blocking any further spread of communism rather than trying to reverse it where it already existed
Invading Eastern Europe to remove the communist governments already installed there
A Soviet policy of surrounding itself with friendly buffer states
hints: The word describes holding something inside a boundary. Ask what the strategy promised to do about the countries already behind that boundary.

problemText: Historians call the fighting in Korea, Vietnam, and Afghanistan during the Cold War 'proxy wars.' What does that term mean?
choices: Wars fought entirely by United Nations peacekeeping forces
Wars in which no weapons or money came from any foreign government
Wars formally declared by treaty between the United States and the Soviet Union
Conflicts in which rival great powers armed and backed opposing sides instead of fighting each other directly
hints: A proxy is someone who acts in your place. Ask who did the actual fighting and who supplied the guns and money.

problemText: In June 1948 the Soviet Union cut every road and rail line into West Berlin, a city of about two million people sitting deep inside the Soviet occupation zone. The Western allies did not send an armed convoy to force the roads open. Instead they supplied the entire city by air for eleven months, until the blockade was lifted. What does that choice best illustrate?
choices: Choosing the response that relieved the city without firing the first shot, leaving the decision to escalate with the other side
The Western allies had no ground forces stationed anywhere in Germany at the time
The United Nations had legally prohibited the movement of supplies into Berlin by land
Flying cargo into a blockaded city was cheaper and simpler than driving it in by truck
hints: Compare the two options by asking who would have to shoot first under each one.

problemText: Stalin installed friendly governments across Eastern Europe and described them as a buffer against a third invasion of Russian territory in thirty years. Washington and London saw the same governments as evidence of expansion and answered with aid and alliances, which Moscow in turn read as an American takeover of Europe. Historians call this pattern a security dilemma. Which statement best defines it?
choices: A situation in which two states share the same goals but lack the treaties to cooperate
A rule of international law requiring states to disarm when a rival does
A situation in which each side's defensive measures look threatening to the other, prompting still more defensive measures
A shortage of weapons that forces a state to rely on allies for its security
hints: Notice that the loop runs in both directions. Ask what happens next when a move meant to feel safe is read as a threat.

problemText: The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 ended with three linked outcomes: the Soviet Union removed its nuclear missiles from Cuba, the United States publicly pledged not to invade Cuba, and the United States quietly withdrew its missiles from Turkey. In 1963 the two governments installed a direct communication link between their leaders. Which conclusion do these outcomes best support?
choices: The crisis showed that nuclear weapons had no real influence on how the two governments behaved
The Soviet Union surrendered completely and received nothing in return for removing the missiles
The United States abandoned its opposition to the Cuban government's alignment with Moscow's bloc
The crisis was settled by mutual concessions, some kept private so that neither leader had to appear defeated at home
hints: Make a two-column list of what each side gave up and what each side received before judging who 'won.'
Ask why one of the three concessions was kept out of the public announcement — what would it have cost the leader who made it?

problemText: In 1957, after years of strikes, party organizing, and negotiation led by Kwame Nkrumah, a British colony in West Africa became independent and took the name Ghana. Which colony was it?
choices: The Gold Coast
Kenya
Algeria
Nigeria
hints: The colony was named for the commodity Europeans had come to the coast to buy.

problemText: In 1930 Mohandas Gandhi walked to the sea and made salt in open violation of the British salt monopoly, then let himself and thousands of followers be arrested for it. Which description best fits the method, called satyagraha?
choices: A guerrilla campaign intended to defeat British forces in battle
Open, nonviolent lawbreaking that accepts punishment so the injustice becomes visible and the rule becomes unworkable
A private appeal to British officials asking them to soften the law
A boycott in which Indians refused to buy goods made in India
hints: Ask why he wanted the arrests to happen in front of an audience rather than avoiding them.

problemText: What was the partition of 1947?
choices: The division of India into British and French administrative zones
A peaceful transfer of power in which no borders moved and no populations relocated
The division of British India into the separate states of India and Pakistan along largely religious lines, followed by roughly a million deaths and about fifteen million people displaced
The separation of Bangladesh from Pakistan following a war between them
hints: Two of these describe real events from other years or other divisions. Fix the year 1947 first, then ask which two states appeared on the map that August.

problemText: In 1956 Egypt's president Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal. Britain and France, joined by Israel, invaded to take it back, and then withdrew after pressure from both the United States and the Soviet Union. Why do historians treat this episode as a turning point for European empire?
choices: It restored British ownership of the canal for another twenty years
It was the first time any colonized population had resisted European rule
It persuaded Egypt to join NATO and align with the Western bloc
It demonstrated publicly that the old imperial powers could no longer act on their own without the superpowers' consent
hints: The military operation itself is less revealing than what ended it. Ask who made Britain and France stop, and what that showed the watching world.

problemText: United Nations membership roughly tripled between 1945 and 1975, and seventeen African nations became independent in the single year 1960. Which explanation best accounts for independence arriving in a cascade rather than a steady trickle?
choices: The colonial powers had signed a treaty in 1945 fixing 1960 as the date on which all colonies would be released
Each success drained the colonizers' will and money while showing other movements that independence was achievable soon, so the pace compounded
The United Nations charter automatically granted independence to any colony that applied for membership
Soviet troops intervened directly in each colony to force the European powers out
hints: Ask what one colony's independence does to the calculations of the colonizer and of the next movement watching it.

problemText: By 1965 a West African state had its own flag, its own elected government, and a seat at the United Nations. It also still earned most of its foreign income from exporting one unprocessed crop, largely to its former colonizer, whose companies did the processing and set much of the price. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The state was in fact still a colony, since independence had never legally taken effect
The colonial economy had been built to feed and employ the local population, and independence disrupted it
Political sovereignty had been achieved while the economic structure built for colonial extraction remained largely intact
This case shows that inherited economic arrangements disappeared quickly once independence was won
hints: Separate the two questions: who holds legal authority over the territory, and who captures the value of what it produces.

problemText: Mikhail Gorbachev became leader of the Soviet Union in 1985 and launched two signature reform policies, one loosening censorship and one restructuring the economy. What were they called?
choices: Containment and detente
Collectivization and the Five-Year Plans
The Brezhnev Doctrine and the Warsaw Pact
Glasnost and perestroika
hints: One of the two words translates as 'openness' and the other as 'restructuring.'

problemText: When a reactor exploded at Chernobyl in April 1986, Soviet officials concealed the scale of the disaster for days while radiation spread. Why is this event so closely tied to the policy of glasnost?
choices: It proved Gorbachev's argument that the system had to stop hiding the truth about itself, while at the same time destroying public trust in official statements
It convinced Gorbachev to reimpose strict censorship and abandon openness
It was the first event that Soviet newspapers had ever been permitted to report
It showed that the Soviet Union had never built any nuclear technology of its own
hints: Glasnost was an argument about secrecy. Ask what a concealed catastrophe does to that argument, and what it does to citizens' willingness to believe the next announcement.

problemText: Which of the following best describes perestroika?
choices: A policy of loosening censorship so that newspapers could discuss the Soviet past
A restructuring of the economy that relaxed central planning and allowed limited private cooperatives and more factory autonomy
A program to expand Soviet missile production to match the United States
A decree abolishing the Communist Party of the Soviet Union
hints: Two of Gorbachev's policies are easy to swap. Ask which one was aimed at speech and which one at factories and prices.

problemText: Gorbachev's economic reforms were meant to end Soviet shortages, yet between 1985 and 1991 shortages and queues grew worse rather than better. Which explanation fits the evidence best?
choices: The reforms dismantled the planning commands that had coordinated supply before any working market existed to take their place
Soviet factories stopped producing goods of any kind after 1985
Every other country imposed a total trade embargo on the Soviet Union in 1985
Central planning was tightened during these years rather than loosened
hints: A system can be coordinated badly or coordinated not at all. Ask what was doing the coordinating before the reforms, and what was doing it during them.

problemText: On the evening of November 9, 1989, an East German official read out new travel rules so confusingly that crowds went straight to the Berlin Wall demanding to cross. Overwhelmed guards opened the gates, and no Soviet troops were sent. Soviet tanks had crushed comparable movements in Hungary in 1956 and Czechoslovakia in 1968. What does the 1989 outcome best illustrate?
choices: The Berlin Wall was demolished by NATO soldiers acting on orders from Western governments
East Germany and West Germany had already legally reunified earlier that year
Once Moscow had withdrawn its promise to use force to keep allied governments in power, a local blunder could no longer be reversed by tanks
The Soviet Union had already dissolved, so no orders could be issued from Moscow at all
hints: Compare 1968 and 1989 and change only one variable at a time. The crowds and the grievances were not the new thing.

problemText: Historians explaining the end of the Cold War weigh four factors against each other: Western military and economic pressure in the early 1980s, Gorbachev's own decisions after 1985, popular movements from Poland's Solidarity to the crowds who faced down the failed Moscow coup of August 1991, and the long-run exhaustion of an economy that could build rockets but not competitive consumer goods or computers. Which assessment is best supported?
choices: American military spending alone accounts for the outcome, and the other three factors can be set aside
Popular movements had no measurable effect, since governments fell only when leaders chose to resign
The Soviet economy was growing strongly through the 1980s, so economic explanations are irrelevant
All four factors contributed, and the decision that most immediately unlocked the revolutions of 1989 was made in Moscow when the threat of Soviet intervention was withdrawn
hints: When several causes are offered, first ask whether the evidence lets you eliminate any of them outright, rather than ranking them straight away.
Distinguish the long-run conditions that made collapse possible from the specific decision that made 1989 happen when it did.

problemText: Beginning in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping, one country introduced market reforms and later opened Special Economic Zones, reorienting its economy toward export manufacturing. Which country was it?
choices: India
China
Brazil
The Soviet Union
hints: A different large Asian economy liberalized in 1991 under different leaders. Fix the 1978 date and the name Deng Xiaoping first.

problemText: Before the mid-1950s, cargo was loaded onto ships sack by sack and crate by crate, and a vessel could sit in port longer than it spent at sea. The change that ended this is called containerization. What is it?
choices: Shipping goods in standardized steel boxes that move between ship, rail, and truck without being unpacked
Building much larger wooden crates so that dockworkers could carry more per trip
Placing ports under government ownership so that loading could be scheduled centrally
Replacing ocean freight with cargo aircraft for most manufactured goods
hints: Ask what has to be true of the box for a crane to move it from a truck to a ship to a train without anyone opening it.

problemText: The World Bank and the International Monetary Fund were created at a conference held at Bretton Woods in 1944. What were they designed to do?
choices: Set production targets for member states' factories and farms
Command and operate international peacekeeping missions
Provide lending and help stabilize currencies so that trade and investment across borders would be predictable
Govern the European Union's shared currency, the euro
hints: Both are financial institutions. Ask what an investor or a government needs to be confident about before committing money across a border.

problemText: Many regions that had never built extensive networks of telephone poles and copper lines moved directly to mobile phone networks, and mobile subscriptions passed roughly one per person worldwide by the mid-2010s. Which conclusion does this pattern best support?
choices: Landline networks were technically impossible to build outside Europe and North America
Mobile networks require more fixed infrastructure per user than landline networks do
Communication technology spread only to countries that had already industrialized
Later adopters can skip an expensive earlier stage of infrastructure, so connection spread faster than the original sequence would have allowed
hints: Ask what it costs to string wire to every house, and whether a region arriving late is obliged to pay that cost first.

problemText: An assembly plant on one continent halted production within days after a major port on another continent closed. Which feature of modern manufacturing does this best illustrate?
choices: Manufacturers generally keep several years of components stockpiled on site
Splitting production across many countries buys efficiency at the price of vulnerability to distant disruptions
International trade today is less interconnected than it was in 1900
Shipping costs make up the largest share of the price of most manufactured goods
hints: Ask what the plant gains by sourcing each part from wherever it is made best or cheapest, and what it gives up by doing so.

problemText: Between about 1990 and 2019 the share of the world's people living in extreme poverty fell from roughly two in five to under one in ten and deaths of children under five roughly halved, while over the same span a number of manufacturing regions in wealthy countries lost factory work and did not regain jobs of comparable pay or security. Which summary of global economic integration is best supported?
choices: The evidence shows that living standards improved at about the same rate for every region and group
The evidence shows that only already-wealthy countries benefited and poverty rates elsewhere were unchanged
The same integration produced very large aggregate gains and sharply concentrated local losses, so an accurate account has to state both halves
The poverty decline occurred almost entirely inside the wealthy countries that also lost factory work
hints: Check each option against both statistics in the prompt. An option that contradicts either one is out.
Aggregate figures and regional figures can point in opposite directions at the same time without either being false.
